samples.answer:
The **best open-source project management tool depends on your workflow**—software development, formal project planning, Scrum, or simple task tracking. As of **October 13, 2026**, these are the strongest options:

| Tool | Best for | Main strengths | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenProject** | Formal, cross-functional project management | Gantt charts, dependencies, budgets, time tracking, roadmaps, Kanban, Scrum, portfolios | More complex to configure |
| **Plane** | Modern software/product teams | Issues, cycles, modules, roadmaps, docs, triage; modern Jira/Linear-style interface | Some advanced capabilities may depend on edition; active, fast-changing project |
| **Redmine** | Mature, customizable issue tracking | Very stable, plugins, workflows, wikis, forums, time tracking, Gantt, Git/SVN integration | Older-looking interface and less polished out of the box |
| **Taiga** | Scrum and Kanban teams | Backlogs, sprints, user stories, Kanban, agile-oriented workflow | Less suited to budgets, resource planning, and formal portfolio management |
| **GitLab Community Edition** | Development teams already using GitLab | Issues, boards, milestones, merge requests, CI/CD, repositories, documentation | Less natural for nontechnical or non-repository-based projects |
| **Vikunja** | Lightweight task and personal/team planning | Lists, Kanban, Gantt, simple project organization, self-hosting | Not as comprehensive for enterprise governance or complex portfolios |
| **Tuleap** | Software lifecycle management and regulated environments | Agile planning, requirements, traceability, testing, and development workflows | More specialized and potentially heavier to administer |

## My recommendations

### 1. Best overall: **OpenProject**

Choose OpenProject if you need a serious general-purpose PM system rather than just an issue tracker. It supports classic, agile, and hybrid methodologies, including work packages, Gantt charts, dependencies, budgets, time and cost reporting, roadmaps, Scrum backlogs, Kanban boards, resource management, and documentation. ([openproject.org](https://www.openproject.org/collaboration-software-features/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** agencies, nonprofits, construction or operations teams, universities, government, and organizations managing multiple projects.

### 2. Best modern Jira/Linear alternative: **Plane**

Plane is a strong choice for software and product teams that want a modern interface for issues, cycles, product roadmaps, modules, docs, and triage. Its Community Edition is open source under AGPLv3 and can be self-hosted. ([github.com](https://github.com/makeplane/plane?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** startups, engineering teams, product managers, and teams migrating from Jira, Linear, Monday, or ClickUp.

### 3. Best mature and extensible option: **Redmine**

Redmine is less fashionable but exceptionally proven and flexible. It supports multiple projects, role-based permissions, custom workflows and fields, Gantt charts, calendars, time tracking, wikis, forums, files, email notifications, and integrations with Git and other source-control systems. It is GPLv2-licensed and self-hostable. ([redmine.org](https://www.redmine.org/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** teams that value stability, plugins, customization, and long-term maintainability over a modern UI.

### 4. Best for Scrum: **Taiga**

Taiga is explicitly designed for agile cross-functional teams using **Scrum or Kanban**. It is a good fit when you want backlogs, sprint planning, and agile boards without the broader governance features of OpenProject. ([taiga.io](https://taiga.io/about-us/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** development, design, and product teams following a relatively conventional agile process.

### 5. Best if your code is already in GitLab: **GitLab**

GitLab works well when project management is closely tied to source code, merge requests, CI/CD, and releases. Its issues support tasks, feature proposals, bugs, labels, due dates, milestones, discussions, templates, and workflows; issue boards support Kanban and Scrum-style processes. ([docs.gitlab.com](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/issues/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** engineering organizations that want planning and delivery in one DevOps platform.

### 6. Best lightweight option: **Vikunja**

Vikunja is a simpler alternative when you mainly need tasks, lists, Kanban boards, and basic project planning. It supports self-hosting and includes list, Kanban, and Gantt-style views. ([vikunja.io](https://vikunja.io/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** individuals, families, small teams, and organizations that find OpenProject or GitLab excessive.

## Quick decision guide

- **Need Gantt charts, budgets, dependencies, and governance?** → **OpenProject**
- **Want a modern Jira or Linear alternative?** → **Plane**
- **Want the most mature plugin ecosystem?** → **Redmine**
- **Run Scrum or Kanban specifically?** → **Taiga**
- **Already use Git repositories and CI/CD?** → **GitLab**
- **Want simple self-hosted task management?** → **Vikunja**
- **Need requirements, testing, traceability, or regulated software development?** → **Tuleap**

One important caveat: “open source” can refer to the whole product, a community edition, or only part of the codebase. Before adopting a tool, check the **license, self-hosted feature set, authentication/SSO availability, backup process, upgrade path, and whether key features are restricted to a commercial edition**. For most teams, I would shortlist **OpenProject, Plane, and Redmine** first.

samples.answer:
**My default recommendation: Asana**—unless your team mainly handles a shared customer/support inbox.

### Best options

| Your situation | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| General team projects and deadlines | **Asana** | Clean task ownership, due dates, projects, dependencies, and views. Gmail/Outlook integrations can turn an email into a task, assign it, set a due date, and add it to a project without leaving the inbox. ([help.asana.com](https://help.asana.com/s/article/use-asana-and-email?nocache=https%3A%2F%2Fhelp.asana.com%2Fs%2Farticle%2Fuse-asana-and-email%3Flanguage%3Des&utm_source=openai)) |
| Your team lives in email and wants email-to-task workflows | **ClickUp** | Forward an email to a List to create a task, preserve attachments, assign it, apply tags, and set due dates using subject-line commands. It can also turn replies into task comments. ([help.clickup.com](https://help.clickup.com/hc/en-us/articles/6309707288599-Create-tasks-and-comments-via-email?utm_source=openai)) |
| Most work arrives in a shared address like `support@` or `sales@` | **Front** | Shared inbox plus linked tasks, assignees, due dates, routing, and conversation history in one place. ([help.front.com](https://help.front.com/en/articles/3244160?utm_source=openai)) |
| You already pay for Microsoft 365 | **Planner + Outlook/Teams** | Planner handles team task boards, while Outlook flags become personal To Do tasks and Planner integrates with Teams and Outlook. ([support.microsoft.com](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/todo/to-do-vs-planner?utm_source=openai)) |
| You need a collaborative inbox rather than a full project-management system | **Missive** | Shared team inboxes, assignments, internal collaboration, task status, and due dates stay attached to the conversation. ([missiveapp.com](https://missiveapp.com/docs/core-features/team-inboxes?utm_source=openai)) |

### What I’d choose for you

Start with **Asana** if the problem is primarily “we discuss work in email and forget to follow up.” Create tasks from important emails, assign one owner, add a real due date, and keep subsequent discussion in the task.

Choose **Front instead** if several people monitor the same inbox and the key question is “who owns this customer email, and has it been resolved?”

### The workflow matters more than the product

Set these rules:

1. **Every actionable email becomes a task.**
2. **Every task has exactly one owner.**
3. **Every task has a due date—or is explicitly marked “no deadline.”**
4. **Replies and decisions go in the task/conversation, not a new email thread.**
5. **Review overdue tasks twice a week.**
6. **Use email only for external communication; use the task system for internal work.**

I’d run a one-week pilot with **Asana and ClickUp**, using 20 real email requests, and compare: how quickly tasks can be created, whether attachments/context are preserved, and whether people actually check their assigned tasks.

([help.asana.com](https://help.asana.com/s/article/use-asana-and-email?nocache=https%3A%2F%2Fhelp.asana.com%2Fs%2Farticle%2Fuse-asana-and-email%3Flanguage%3Des&utm_source=openai))

|---|---|

| You want a very simple visual board | **Trello**—easy to adopt, with built-in automation; paid plans currently start at $5/user/month annually. ([trello.com](https://trello.com/en-US/pricing?eco_tools=CRM_EMAIL_TEMPLATES&utm_source=openai)) |

Whichever tool you choose, establish these rules:

1. **No deadline-only commitments in email.** If it requires action, create a task.
2. Every task must have **one owner and one due date**.
3. Use a standard workflow: **Inbox → Next → In progress → Waiting → Done**.

## My recommendation

### 1. **Microsoft Planner + Outlook/Teams** — best if you already use Microsoft 365
Choose this if your team lives in Outlook and Teams.

([support.microsoft.com](https://support.microsoft.com/en-au/todo/using-microsoft-to-do-with-flagged-email-from-outlook?utm_source=openai))

### 2. **Asana** — best general-purpose choice for most teams
Choose this if you want a clean, dedicated task system that works across departments.

- Convert an email into an Asana task from Outlook.
- Assign an owner, set a due date, attach the email context, and place it in a project.
- Supports due dates, due times, start dates, recurring tasks, dependencies, and project views. ([asana.com](https://asana.com/inside-asana/new-asana-outlook-integration?utm_source=openai))

Asana is probably my default recommendation for a team that has outgrown email but does not need highly complex project management.

### 3. **ClickUp** — best if email-to-task automation is central
Choose this if your team wants to forward emails directly into task lists.

- Each ClickUp List can have a unique email address.
- The email subject becomes the task name and the body becomes the description.
- You can include assignment and due-date tags, such as `<assign person@example.com>` and `<due next Friday>`.
- Attachments can be added to the task, and replies can become task comments. ([help.clickup.com](https://help.clickup.com/hc/en-us/articles/6309707288599-Create-tasks-and-comments-via-email?utm_source=openai))

ClickUp is powerful, but it may require more setup and governance than Asana.

If your team handles customer requests, vendor inquiries, support, or operations through a shared mailbox, consider a shared-inbox product rather than a traditional project manager.

## The workflow that prevents missed deadlines

Regardless of software, enforce this rule:

> No task is considered actionable until it has an owner, a due date, and a clearly written next action.

For each actionable email:

1. Create or convert it into a task.
2. Assign exactly one accountable owner.
3. Set a due date and, when useful, a due time.
4. Attach or link the original email.
5. Put it in a shared project/list—not someone’s private inbox.
6. Review overdue and due-soon tasks during a short weekly meeting.
7. Archive or label the email after the task exists elsewhere.

Avoid adopting a system where people merely flag emails. That preserves the same underlying problem: deadlines remain hidden in individual inboxes rather than visible to the team.

**2. Asana — best general-purpose choice for project/task management**  
Use Asana if email is only the intake point and your team needs projects, dependencies, timelines, recurring processes, and clear accountability. Emails can be forwarded into Asana as tasks, and Asana supports assignees, due dates, dependencies, rules, and timeline views. ([asana.com](https://asana.com/resources/asana-email-tips?utm_source=openai))

**3. Microsoft Planner — best if your company already uses Microsoft 365**  
Planner integrates naturally with Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 365. Outlook-flagged emails can appear as tasks, while Planner provides shared team plans, assignments, progress charts, and deadline notifications. ([support.microsoft.com](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/todo/to-do-vs-planner?utm_source=openai))

**4. Trello — best for a simple visual workflow**  
Trello is a good low-complexity option: forward an email to a board to create a card, retain the original email, and use lists such as “New,” “In progress,” “Waiting,” and “Done.” ([support.atlassian.com](https://support.atlassian.com/trello/docs/creating-cards-by-email/?utm_source=openai))

### What I’d choose

- **Email-heavy operations or customer service:** Front  
- **Most internal teams:** Asana  
- **Already paying for Microsoft 365:** Planner  
- **Small team wanting simplicity:** Trello  

### The important part: enforce one workflow

Whatever you choose, establish these rules:

1. **Every task has one owner.**
2. **Every task has a due date—or is explicitly marked “no deadline.”**
3. **The email thread is converted into a task, not left as the task system.**
4. **Status is visible:** New → In progress → Waiting → Done.
5. **No “reply all” updates for task status**; updates go in the task.
6. **Review overdue tasks twice a week.**

If you want one answer without evaluating further: **start with Asana**, unless your team primarily manages shared customer or departmental inboxes—in that case, choose **Front**. Run a two-week pilot with one team and a single project before migrating everything.

## My recommendations

### 1. Best overall: **OpenProject**

Choose OpenProject if you need a serious, general-purpose PM system rather than just an issue tracker. It supports both traditional and agile project management, including work packages, roadmaps, Gantt charts, boards, budgets, time/cost tracking, team planning, reports, and wikis. It is GPLv3 and has a self-installed Community edition. ([openproject.org](https://www.openproject.org/docs/getting-started/openproject-introduction/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** construction, consulting, agencies, nonprofits, internal PMOs, and organizations managing multiple projects.

### 2. Best modern alternative to Jira: **Plane**

Plane is a strong choice for software and product teams that want a newer, cleaner interface. Its open-source repository describes support for tasks, sprints/cycles, docs, triage, and product roadmaps, and it is licensed under AGPL-3.0. ([github.com](https://github.com/makeplane/plane?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** engineering, product, startup, and design teams that prefer a Linear-like workflow.

### 3. Best for Scrum/Kanban: **Taiga**

Taiga is specifically oriented toward agile teams using Scrum and Kanban. Its official documentation emphasizes agile project management, REST API support, Docker deployment, and integrations with services such as GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Slack. ([docs.taiga.io](https://docs.taiga.io/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** development teams that want a focused agile tool without the breadth of OpenProject.

### 4. Best mature and extensible option: **Redmine**

Redmine remains an excellent choice if stability, customization, and a long-lived installation matter more than modern UI. It supports multiple projects, role-based permissions, configurable workflows, custom fields, Gantt charts, calendars, time tracking, wikis, forums, documents, and Git/SVN/Mercurial integration. ([redmine.org](https://www.redmine.org/projects/redmine/wiki/Features?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** technical teams, universities, IT departments, and organizations willing to configure plugins or customize Ruby on Rails.

### 5. Best lightweight option: **Vikunja**

Vikunja is better thought of as a self-hosted task and project manager than a full PMO suite. It provides list, Kanban, Gantt, and table views, project hierarchies, sharing, and task migration tools. The core self-hosted version is AGPLv3. ([vikunja.io](https://vikunja.io/?utm_source=openai))

One caveat: some organizational features, including the admin panel, audit logs, and time tracking, are offered through Vikunja Pro rather than the base AGPL version. ([vikunja.io](https://vikunja.io/docs/pro/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** individuals, small teams, homelabs, and teams that want something simpler than Jira or OpenProject.

### 6. Best for non-project managers: **Leantime**

Leantime focuses on making project management approachable for people who do not identify as project managers. Its open-source feature set includes Kanban, Gantt, calendar, milestones, goals, dashboards, docs, retrospectives, time tracking, risk analysis, and strategy canvases. ([github.com](https://github.com/leantime/leantime?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:** small businesses, creative teams, nonprofits, and teams that want planning and strategy alongside task management.

## Quick decision guide

- **Need Gantt charts, budgets, resources, and formal reporting?** → **OpenProject**
- **Need a modern Jira/Linear replacement for software development?** → **Plane**
- **Use strict Scrum or Kanban?** → **Taiga**
- **Want maximum maturity and plugin flexibility?** → **Redmine**
- **Want a simple self-hosted task manager?** → **Vikunja**
- **Want business planning and goals for a nontechnical team?** → **Leantime**

**My default shortlist:** Start with **OpenProject**, **Plane**, and **Vikunja**. They cover the broadest range—from full-scale project governance to modern software delivery to lightweight task management. Before committing, check the exact license and whether features such as SSO, audit logs, time tracking, or advanced reporting are included in the self-hosted edition.

| Tool | Free-plan limit | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **ClickUp** | Unlimited members and tasks; 60 MB storage; includes Docs, Kanban boards, calendar, sprints, and basic custom fields. ([clickup.com](https://clickup.com/pricing?targetid=aud-1079040687808%3Akwd-378487153917&utm_source=openai)) | Teams wanting the most features for free |
| **Trello** | Up to 10 collaborators per Workspace; useful core board and card features. ([trello.com](https://trello.com/en-US/pricing?eco_tools=CRM_EMAIL_TEMPLATES&utm_source=openai)) | Simple Kanban boards and task tracking |
| **Jira** | Up to 10 users; unlimited projects and work items; Scrum/Kanban boards; 2 GB storage; 100 automation runs per month. ([wac-cdn-a.atlassian.com](https://wac-cdn-a.atlassian.com/software/jira/guides/more/jira-editions?utm_source=openai)) | Software-development and Agile teams |
| **Linear** | Unlimited members, 2 teams, and 250 issues; 10 MB file-upload limit. ([linear.app](https://linear.app/pricing)) | Product and engineering teams |
| **Asana** | Free for up to 2 users, with unlimited tasks and projects plus list, board, and calendar views. ([asana.com](https://asana.com/pricing?gspk=ZXJpbmdpYnNvbjkxOTM&gsxid=6Pdq18FwAvJW&utm_source=openai)) | Very small teams that prefer a polished task manager |
| **monday.com** | Free forever for up to 2 seats, with up to 3 boards and 3 Docs. ([monday.com](https://monday.com/pricing)) | Visual workflows and lightweight operations tracking |
| **Basecamp** | One active project, up to 5 users, and 1 GB storage. ([basecamp.com](https://basecamp.com/pricing?tp=1&utm_source=openai)) | A small team managing one ongoing project |
| **Notion** | Free workspace with unlimited pages for individuals, but limited blocks when multiple members collaborate; 10 external guests and 5 MB file uploads. ([notion.so](https://www.notion.so/pricing)) | Teams combining project tracking, documentation, and notes |

### My short recommendations

- **Best overall free plan:** **ClickUp**
- **Simplest to start:** **Trello**
- **Best for developers:** **Jira** or **Linear**
- **Best for documentation-heavy work:** **Notion**
- **Best for one small project:** **Basecamp**
- **Best for only two collaborators:** **Asana** or **monday.com**

The main caution is that “free” varies substantially: **ClickUp, Trello, Jira, and Linear** are generally the strongest choices if you have more than two internal team members, while **Asana and monday.com currently cap their free plans at two seats**.

The **best Gantt-chart tool depends on whether you prioritize scheduling depth, ease of use, or broader project management**. My shortlist:

| Tool | Best for | Why its Gantt chart stands out | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TeamGantt** | Most teams that want a dedicated Gantt tool | Very intuitive drag-and-drop planning, dependencies, milestones, critical path, baselines, workload views, and stakeholder sharing. ([teamgantt.com](https://www.teamgantt.com/platform/?utm_source=openai)) | Less robust than enterprise tools for complex budgeting and portfolio governance |
| **Microsoft Planner / Project** | Microsoft 365 organizations and complex schedules | Timeline/Gantt views, advanced dependency types, automatic schedule updates, critical-path filtering, milestones, and deep Microsoft 365 integration. ([support.microsoft.com](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/planner/teams/manage-your-team-s-plans-with-planner-in-teams?utm_source=openai)) | Premium features and the scheduling model can be confusing; more powerful tiers are needed for serious planning |
| **GanttPRO** | Gantt-first planning at a relatively low per-user cost | Strong dependency management, critical path, baselines, imports from Microsoft Project/Excel, and polished exports. ([teamgantt.com](https://www.teamgantt.com/gantt-chart-software?utm_source=openai)) | More limited as an all-purpose collaboration workspace |
| **Smartsheet** | Operations teams and spreadsheet-heavy organizations | Combines spreadsheet-like editing with Gantt charts, dependencies, reporting, resource views, and portfolio-level visibility. ([capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/resources/project-management-software-with-gantt-chart/?utm_source=openai)) | Can become expensive and administratively complex at scale |
| **ClickUp** | Teams wanting tasks, docs, dashboards, and Gantt in one system | Supports all four standard dependency types, automatic rescheduling, critical-path views, and a broad task-management platform. ([clickup.com](https://clickup.com/learn/topic/project-management/tools/features/gantt-charts/?utm_source=openai)) | Gantt is one feature among many, so the experience can feel busy |
| **Asana or monday.com** | Teams that mainly need a visual timeline | Easy-to-use timeline/Gantt-style views and strong collaboration around tasks. They’re good for lighter schedules, but generally less schedule-centric than TeamGantt, GanttPRO, or Microsoft’s premium planning tools. ([capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/resources/project-management-software-with-gantt-chart/?utm_source=openai)) | Advanced scheduling features may require higher plans or may be less deep |

### My practical recommendations

- **Best overall for most small and midsize teams:** **TeamGantt**
- **Best for professional schedulers and complex dependencies:** **Microsoft Planner’s premium capabilities / Microsoft Project**
- **Best dedicated Gantt alternative:** **GanttPRO**
- **Best for spreadsheet-oriented companies:** **Smartsheet**
- **Best all-in-one work-management platform:** **ClickUp**
- **Best if you already use Microsoft 365:** **Planner**, especially if you need Teams integration

When evaluating a Gantt chart, test whether it supports **dependency cascading, all four dependency types, milestones, critical-path highlighting, baselines, workload/capacity planning, and easy sharing with people who do not have a license**. Those features distinguish a true scheduling tool from a simple timeline view. ([teamgantt.com](https://www.teamgantt.com/gantt-chart-software?utm_source=openai))
